title: Gemcitabine + cisplatin · 28-day schedule
purpose: Help control advanced urothelial cancer and its symptoms.
schedule_summary: Gemcitabine is given on days 1, 8 and 15. Cisplatin is usually given after gemcitabine on day 1; the source also permits day 2. The cycle repeats every 28 days, usually for four to six cycles. Your unit confirms your actual cisplatin day and appointments.
administration_text: Gemcitabine runs into a vein over 30 minutes. Cisplatin runs over 60 minutes with prescribed fluids before and after. Tests, pharmacy preparation, review and support medicines add to the visit time.
monitoring_summary: Full blood count, kidney and liver tests on day 1; blood count and creatinine before day 8. Day-15 treatment also needs review against the intracycle count and toxicity criteria; your unit confirms the required tests. Check symptoms before every dose.
safety_note: Follow your own prescription and hospital instructions. This information supports a discussion; it does not authorise treatment.
urgent_extra: Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

agents.name: Gemcitabine
agents.explanation: Gemcitabine interferes with making DNA, which dividing cancer cells need. Healthy blood-forming cells and other tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Report fever, unusual bleeding, breathlessness, rash, swelling or reduced urine promptly.
risks: Low blood counts, serious infection, anaemia and bleeding
Nausea, vomiting, fatigue, flu-like symptoms and swelling
Rash, sore mouth and liver-test changes
Uncommon or rare serious lung inflammation, kidney injury including haemolytic uraemic syndrome, severe skin reactions and capillary leak

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. Kidney protection with fluids and monitoring is central to cisplatin treatment.
agents.watch: Report ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Tell the team if you cannot drink, are passing less urine or become swollen or breathless during fluids.
risks: Kidney injury and low magnesium or other electrolyte changes
Hearing loss or ringing in the ears, which may be lasting
Numbness or tingling from nerve damage, sometimes lasting
Low blood counts, serious infection and bleeding

anatomy: Call urgently for new cough or breathlessness.

Blood tests check liver function; report yellow eyes or dark urine.
Follow the anti-sickness plan; call if unable to keep fluids down.
Report reduced urine or new swelling; keep kidney blood tests.
Fever, sudden illness or unusual bleeding needs urgent advice.
Report widespread rash, blistering or peeling urgently.

evidence.title: GemCis versus MVAC (2000)
evidence.summary: A randomised trial in previously untreated advanced urothelial cancer compared 28-day gemcitabine/cisplatin with MVAC. Response rates were 49% and 46%; overall survival did not differ significantly (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% confidence interval 0.82–1.32).
evidence.intro: A randomised trial in previously untreated advanced urothelial cancer compared 28-day gemcitabine/cisplatin with MVAC. Response rates were 49% and 46%; overall survival did not differ significantly (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% confidence interval 0.82–1.32).
evidence.caveat: The study did not prove every GemCis schedule equivalent. It used cisplatin on day 2 and predates newer systemic options. Group averages cannot predict an individual outcome.
evidence.interpretation: The study did not prove every GemCis schedule equivalent. It used cisplatin on day 2 and predates newer systemic options. Group averages cannot predict an individual outcome.

questions.a: No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.
